steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision / robotics paper presenting FoundationPose, our unified method for 6D pose estimation and tracking of novel objects. It should explain the limits of instance-level and category-level methods, the model-based vs model-free setups, pose tracking, and end with our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Object pose estimation: what it is, why it matters; instance-level and category-level methods and their limits
- Recent work on novel objects: model-based vs model-free setups; need for a unified method
- Pose tracking as a related problem with the same issues
- Our method FoundationPose: what it does and how it generalizes
- Contributions list
- Code/data release

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Object pose estimation
  - computing rigid 6D transformation object -> camera
  - crucial for robotic manipulation (cite), mixed reality (cite)
  - classic methods (cite) = instance-level: only work on specific object instance fixed at training time
  - usually need textured CAD model to generate training data; can't handle unseen novel object at test time
  - category-level methods (cite): remove these assumptions (instance-wise training, CAD models) but limited to the predefined category they're trained on
  - category-level training data notoriously hard to get, partly due to extra pose canonicalization and examination steps (cite)
- Novel objects
  - recent efforts: instant pose estimation of arbitrary novel objects (cite)
  - two setups depending on info at test time: model-based (textured 3D CAD model given), model-free (set of reference images given)
  - progress on each setup separately; still need single method for both in a unified way, since real applications provide different info
- Pose tracking
  - orthogonal to single-frame estimation; tracking methods (cite) use temporal cues -> more efficient, smooth, accurate pose on video
  - share the same issues as pose estimation counterparts, depending on assumptions about object knowledge
- FoundationPose
  - unified framework: pose estimation + tracking, novel objects, model-based + model-free, RGBD images
  - outperforms state-of-art methods specialized for each of the four tasks (Fig. 1)
  - generalizability: large-scale synthetic training aided by LLM; novel transformer-based architecture; contrastive learning
  - neural implicit representation bridges model-based/model-free: novel view synthesis from small number (\sim 16) of reference images
  - rendering much faster than previous render-and-compare methods (cite)
- Contributions
  - unified framework, both setups; object-centric neural implicit representation bridges the gap
  - LLM-aided synthetic data generation pipeline; more variety of 3D training assets via diverse texture augmentation
  - transformer-based network architectures + contrastive learning formulation -> strong generalization trained only on synthetic data
  - outperforms specialized methods by large margin across multiple public datasets; even comparable to instance-level methods with fewer assumptions
- code and data will be released

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Object pose estimation means computing the rigid 6D transformation from the object to the camera. It is crucial for a lot of applications, like robotic manipulation and mixed reality. Classic methods are called instance-level, because they only work on the specific object instance that was determined at training time. These methods usually need a textured CAD model to generate the training data, and they can't be applied to an unseen novel object at test time. Category-level methods remove these assumptions (instance-wise training and CAD models), but then they are limited to objects in the predefined category they were trained on. Also, getting category-level training data is notoriously hard, partly because of the extra pose canonicalization and examination steps that have to be applied.

To deal with these limitations, more recent work has focused on instant pose estimation of arbitrary novel objects. There are two setups, depending on what information is available at test time. In the model-based setup a textured 3D CAD model of the object is given, and in the model-free setup a set of reference images of the object is given. A lot of progress has been made on each setup on its own, but there is still a need for a single method that addresses both setups in a unified way, because different real-world applications give different types of information.

Separately from single-frame pose estimation, there are also pose tracking methods that use temporal cues to make pose estimation on a video sequence more efficient, smooth and accurate. These methods have similar issues to the pose estimation methods mentioned above, depending on what they assume about the object knowledge.

- FoundationPose
  - unified framework: pose estimation + tracking, novel objects, model-based + model-free, RGBD images
  - outperforms state-of-art methods specialized for each of the four tasks (Fig. 1)
  - generalizability: large-scale synthetic training aided by LLM; novel transformer-based architecture; contrastive learning
  - neural implicit representation bridges model-based/model-free: novel view synthesis from small number (\sim 16) of reference images
  - rendering much faster than previous render-and-compare methods (cite)
- Contributions
  - unified framework, both setups; object-centric neural implicit representation bridges the gap
  - LLM-aided synthetic data generation pipeline; more variety of 3D training assets via diverse texture augmentation
  - transformer-based network architectures + contrastive learning formulation -> strong generalization trained only on synthetic data
  - outperforms specialized methods by large margin across multiple public datasets; even comparable to instance-level methods with fewer assumptions
- code and data will be released

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Object pose estimation means computing the rigid 6D transformation from the object to the camera. It is crucial for a lot of applications, like robotic manipulation and mixed reality. Classic methods are called instance-level, because they only work on the specific object instance that was determined at training time. These methods usually need a textured CAD model to generate the training data, and they can't be applied to an unseen novel object at test time. Category-level methods remove these assumptions (instance-wise training and CAD models), but then they are limited to objects in the predefined category they were trained on. Also, getting category-level training data is notoriously hard, partly because of the extra pose canonicalization and examination steps that have to be applied.

To deal with these limitations, more recent work has focused on instant pose estimation of arbitrary novel objects. There are two setups, depending on what information is available at test time. In the model-based setup a textured 3D CAD model of the object is given, and in the model-free setup a set of reference images of the object is given. A lot of progress has been made on each setup on its own, but there is still a need for a single method that addresses both setups in a unified way, because different real-world applications give different types of information.

Separately from single-frame pose estimation, there are also pose tracking methods that use temporal cues to make pose estimation on a video sequence more efficient, smooth and accurate. These methods have similar issues to the pose estimation methods mentioned above, depending on what they assume about the object knowledge.

In this paper we propose FoundationPose, a unified framework that does both pose estimation and tracking for novel objects, in both the model-based and the model-free setups, using RGBD images. Our method outperforms the existing state-of-art methods that are specialized for each of these four tasks, as can be seen in Fig. 1. The strong generalizability comes from large-scale synthetic training aided by a large language model (LLM), and also from a novel transformer-based architecture and contrastive learning. To bridge the gap between the model-based and model-free setups we use a neural implicit representation. This allows effective novel view synthesis with a small number (\sim 16) of reference images, and the rendering speed is significantly faster than previous render-and-compare methods. Our contributions are the following:

- We present a unified framework for pose estimation and tracking of novel objects that supports both model-based and model-free setups. The gap between the two setups is bridged by an object-centric neural implicit representation for effective novel view synthesis.

- We propose a synthetic data generation pipeline aided by an LLM, which scales up the variety of 3D training assets with diverse texture augmentation.

- Our novel transformer-based network architectures and contrastive learning formulation give strong generalization when trained only on synthetic data.

- Our method outperforms existing methods specialized for each task by a large margin on multiple public datasets. It even gets results comparable to instance-level methods, even though it makes fewer assumptions.

Code and data from this work will be released.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Computing the rigid 6D transformation from the object to the camera, also known as object pose estimation, is crucial for a variety of applications, such as robotic manipulation [1,2,3] and mixed reality [4]. Classic methods [5,6,7,8,9] are known as instance-level because they only work on the specific object instance determined at training time. Such methods usually require a textured CAD model to generate training data, and they cannot be applied to an unseen novel object at test time. While category-level methods [10,11,12,13,14] remove these assumptions (instance-wise training and CAD models), they are limited to objects within the predefined category they are trained on. Moreover, obtaining category-level training data is notoriously difficult, in part because of the additional pose canonicalization and examination steps [10] that must be applied.

To address these limitations, more recent efforts have focused on the problem of instant pose estimation of arbitrary novel objects [15,16,17,18,19]. Two different setups are considered, depending on what information is available at test time: model-based, where a textured 3D CAD model of the object is provided, and model-free, where a set of reference images of the object is provided. While much progress has been made on each setup individually, there is still a need for a single method that addresses both setups in a unified way, since different real-world applications provide different types of information.

Orthogonal to single-frame object pose estimation, pose tracking methods [20,21,22,23,24,25,26,27] leverage temporal cues to make pose estimation on a video sequence more efficient, smooth and accurate. Depending on their assumptions about the object knowledge, these methods share similar issues to their counterparts in pose estimation.

In this paper we propose a unified framework called FoundationPose that performs both pose estimation and tracking for novel objects in both the model-based and model-free setups, using RGBD images. As seen in Fig. 1, our method outperforms existing state-of-art methods specialized for each of these four tasks. Our strong generalizability is achieved through large-scale synthetic training aided by a large language model (LLM), together with a novel transformer-based architecture and contrastive learning. We bridge the gap between the model-based and model-free setups with a neural implicit representation that allows effective novel view synthesis from a small number (\sim 16) of reference images, with rendering speeds significantly faster than previous render-and-compare methods [23,16,20]. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- We present a unified framework for both pose estimation and tracking of novel objects, supporting both model-based and model-free setups. An object-centric neural implicit representation for effective novel view synthesis bridges the gap between the two setups.

- We propose an LLM-aided synthetic data generation pipeline that scales up the variety of 3D training assets through diverse texture augmentation.

- Our novel design of transformer-based network architectures and contrastive learning formulation leads to strong generalization when trained only on synthetic data.

- Our method outperforms existing methods specialized for each task by a large margin across multiple public datasets, and even achieves results comparable to instance-level methods despite reduced assumptions.

Code and data developed in this work will be released.
